cover.intro: Document templates are the reusable layouts behind every contract, proposal, booking and customer document in Nexudus. You write the layout once, fill it with fields for the real values, and Nexudus generates a finished, personalised document each time you need one. This course covers creating a template and writing it in the Document Designer.
objectives: Create a document template and choose the right editor and data context for it
Write a document in the Document Designer, inserting fields, conditions, repeats and signature lines
Preview and generate documents from a template for the right kind of record
cover.disclaimer: The content and images in this course are accurate as of publication but may change over time. Images are for illustration only and may differ from what appears on your system.

blocks.html: A document template lives under Sales & relationships › Document Templates. It is a layout you write once and generate from many times: a membership agreement, a booking confirmation, a welcome letter or a proposal covering note. In this lesson you will see the templates list, the three kinds of template, and the three-step wizard that creates a new one.

The list opens sorted by name and shows each template’s Template name, its Editor, what it is About, and its Location. The Editor badge says how the template is written (Designer or Classic); the About badge says what data it can see (Customer, Contract, Proposal, Booking or Not set).

blocks.alt: The Document Templates list showing the Editor and About columns

blocks.html: The template name is not just a label: it becomes the file name of every document generated from it, so “Membership agreement” gives a customer a file they can recognise and “Template 3” does not. Two row commands are available on each template: Preview template generates a document from sample data and downloads it without touching a customer, and Copy template makes an exact copy named “… - Copy”. There is no versioning, so copying is how a second version starts.
Every template is one of three things, and which one is decided when you create it:

items.title: Designer
items.html: The default choice, written in the Document Designer inside Flow. It is the only editor where you pick fields from a list, add conditions and repeats, place signature lines, and see a live preview. Use it almost always.

items.title: Classic HTML
items.html: Written as HTML with Liquid in a code editor inside Flow, for example {{ Coworker.FullName }} for a value and {% if %} for a condition. Choose this when you already have working HTML and Liquid, or need something the Designer cannot express.

items.title: Word
items.html: An uploaded .docx with merge fields, edited in Microsoft Word rather than in Flow. Choose this when you have a .docx that must stay a .docx. An uploaded Word file must be 10 MB or smaller.

blocks.html: The editor type and what the document is about are both set once, at creation, on a Designer template. There is no way to turn a Classic template into a Designer one, and going the other way (Detach) throws the design away. Getting these two right at creation is worth a minute’s thought — everything else about a template can be changed later.

Every template names one thing it is about, and that single choice decides three things at once: which fields exist, which record the preview uses, and which starters you are offered. The customer and the location are available in all four; the rest is added by the choice.

items.title: Customer
items.html: General documents for a customer: their details, company, team and your location. It has no single contract to point at, so it cannot print a plan name, price or start date.

items.title: Contract
items.html: Agreements for a customer contract: the plan, price, term, deposits and products, plus the customer. A membership agreement is about a Contract, not a Customer.

items.title: Proposal
items.html: Documents sent with or signed for a proposal: its products, plans, totals and validity, plus the customer.

items.title: Booking
items.html: Confirmations for a booking: the resource, times, guests, extras and cost, plus the customer.

blocks.html: Choosing the wrong one is the commonest reason a template cannot say what you want. Pick Customer and the plan, price and term are not in the field list at all. Ask which single record the document is generated from, and match the choice to it.
Click Create document template to open a three-step wizard rather than a form.

blocks.intro: Follow these steps to create a new document template.
steps: Navigate to Sales & relationships › Document Templates and click Create document template.
Name the template and pick the Location it belongs to. The name is shown to your team and used as the file name of generated documents.
Say what it is about: Customer, Contract, Proposal or Booking. Each card explains what data that choice gives the template.
Choose where to start: A starter, A blank page, A Word document, or HTML or Liquid. The card you pick decides which editor the template gets for the rest of its life.
Finish the wizard to open the template in its editor, ready to edit.
blocks.summary: A starter is copied, not linked: editing it afterwards changes only your template, and a later improvement to the starter never reaches templates already made from it.

blocks.alt: Step two of the create wizard: choosing what the document is about

questions.prompt: You need a membership agreement that prints the member's plan, price and term. What should the template be about?
questions.correctFeedback: Correct — a membership agreement is about a Contract, which adds the plan, price and term.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite — only a Contract template can see the plan, price and term. A Customer template has no single contract to point at.

questions.prompt: Which row command lets you check a template without touching a customer?
questions.correctFeedback: Correct — Preview template generates a document from sample data and downloads it; nothing is sent to a customer.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite — Preview template is the safe rehearsal. It works on every kind of template, Word included.

questions.prompt: A Word template can be converted into a Designer template at any time.
questions.correctFeedback: Correct — there is no way to turn a Classic (including Word) template into a Designer one. Convert to Designer exists on a Word template but is not available yet.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite — the editor type is fixed at creation for Designer templates, and Classic templates cannot be turned into Designer ones.

questions.prompt: An uploaded Word file must be ______ MB or smaller.
questions.correctFeedback: Correct — anything larger than 10 MB is refused.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite — the limit is 10 MB; a .docx full of images is the usual cause of going over it.

questions.prompt: Why does the template name matter beyond being a label?
options: It is used for search ranking
It becomes the file name of every document generated from it
It determines which editor is used
questions.correctFeedback: Correct — the name becomes the file name of every generated document, so give it a recognisable name.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite — the name becomes the file name of every document generated from the template.

blocks.html: The Document Designer is a word processor that knows your data. Type as you would anywhere, and where the document needs a real value — a name, a price, a date — insert a field instead of typing it. In this lesson you will learn the layout, how to insert and set up fields, how to add conditions and repeats, how to place signature lines, and how to preview and save.

The Designer has five areas: the header (the template name, Preview, Save and More actions); the toolbar with two tabs (Format for text, Document for the page) and Insert at the end; the outline on the left; the page in the middle; and three side tabs on the right: Fields, Selection and AI.

blocks.alt: The Document Designer: header, toolbar, outline, page and the three side tabs

blocks.html: A document has three places text can live: the page header (repeats at the top of every page), the body (the document itself), and the page footer (repeats at the bottom of every page). Page numbers and page counts belong in the header or footer — put one in the body and it prints once, in the middle of the text.

A field is a hole in the document that the real value drops into. Put the cursor exactly where the value goes, search the Fields tab (it matches the label and the path), and choose the field. It appears as a chip, for example Contract › Price.

blocks.intro: Insert a field from your data.
steps: Put the cursor where the value belongs — a field is inserted at the cursor, mid-sentence if that is where you are.
Search Search fields… in the Fields tab. Fields are grouped (Location, Customer, Contract) and each shows its kind and an example.
Choose the field to insert it at the cursor.
Select the chip to open Selection and set its Format, Transform and When empty, show.

blocks.html: Give a fallback (“When empty, show”) to every field that is not guaranteed — a company name, a second line of an address, an end date on an open-ended contract. It stops a blank looking like a mistake. Money fields already have money formatting applied automatically, so do not add it again.
One agreement has to cover the customer with a deposit and the one without. Two blocks do that:

items.title: Show when…
items.html: Wraps content in a rule. When the rule is true the content prints; when it is false, whatever is under Otherwise prints instead. Match is all of these or any of these. is not empty on a list is how you ask “does this customer have any deposits at all?”

items.title: Repeat for each…
items.html: Prints its content once per item in a list (deposits, products, guests). Call each item names the fields inside the block — with the name deposit, the field is deposit › Name. An empty branch covers what prints when the list has nothing in it.

items.title: Repeating table rows
items.html: A table can repeat one row per item instead of wrapping the whole table. Repeat rows… marks one row as the template row — a header row that stays put and a body row that multiplies. This is what a deposits or products table wants.

blocks.html: A signature line is a block like any other: insert it where people sign and say who it belongs to. Signer number matters — the customer is always signer 1, and additional signatories follow in the order they are listed on the customer file. One signer usually needs more than one block (a signature and a date beside it); give both the same signer number.

A signer with no line still signs — somewhere you did not choose. A document sent to three people with two lines comes back with an extra signature page appended. Check the Signatures summary at the foot of the outline against who will actually be asked to sign.

The right-hand end of the toolbar always says how the design stands: Everything looks good, N suggestions, or N problems to fix before saving. Problems block saving and the preview — the commonest is a field that no longer exists.

Preview (in the header) answers the only question that matters before a document goes out: what will the customer actually receive? Choose Sample data to check wording, or A real record to check reality — ideally an awkward one with the least filled in. Switch Preview as from Page to PDF: the PDF, not the canvas, decides page breaks and where signature fields land.

blocks.alt: The preview window in PDF mode, reporting how many signature fields were placed

blocks.html: Nothing is saved as you type — click Save in the header. The Designer keeps unsaved work in the browser, so a template you left unsaved offers to restore it, but that draft survives only the open tab. Render the PDF before sending anything for signature.

A template becomes a real document in three places: a customer file (where signatures are collected), a proposal (the two documents it carries), or the Create document action on a customer, contract or booking. Run Create document from the record the template is about — a Contract template run from a customer has no contract to read, so the plan, price and term come out empty.

questions.prompt: Where do page numbers and page counts belong in a Designer document?
options: In the page header or footer
questions.correctFeedback: Correct — headers and footers repeat on every page, so that is where page numbers belong.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite — put a page number in the body and it prints once, in the middle of the text. Use the header or footer.

questions.prompt: How do you ask whether a customer has any deposits at all?
options: A Show when… condition with 'is not empty' on the deposits list
questions.correctFeedback: Correct — 'is not empty' on a list is the condition around almost every deposits section.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite — use a Show when… condition with 'is not empty' on the deposits list.

questions.prompt: A field that no longer resolves to your data is a problem that blocks saving.
questions.correctFeedback: Correct — an unknown field is a problem, so Save is refused until you re-pick the field.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite — an unknown field is a problem and blocks saving until you fix it.

questions.prompt: A document is sent for e-signature to three people but the design has only two signature lines. What happens?
options: Dropbox Sign appends its own signature page for the missing signer
The third signer is silently skipped
questions.correctFeedback: Correct — a signer with no line still signs; Dropbox Sign adds its own signature page for them.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite — the missing signer still signs, on an extra signature page Dropbox Sign appends.

questions.prompt: You want to check what an actual customer's document will look like, including an empty company name. Which preview option do you use?
questions.correctFeedback: Correct — a real record is the only way to see what an actual customer's document looks like when a field is empty.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite — sample data fills every field, so it hides empties. Use a real record, ideally an awkward one.

questions.prompt: The button in the Designer header that renders the real file and reports how many signature fields were placed is the ______ preview.
questions.correctFeedback: Correct — the PDF preview renders the real thing and reports the signature field count.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Not quite — it is the PDF preview, not the Page preview, that settles page breaks and signature placement.

blocks.html:
You should now be able to:

  • Create a document template and choose the right editor and data context for it
  • Write a document in the Document Designer, inserting fields, conditions, repeats and signature lines
  • Preview and generate documents from a template for the right kind of record
